Opposition, treasury in Sindh Assembly unite to demand Centre stop daily petroleum price hikes. • PTI resolution states daily fluctuations in global oil prices should not be passed on to consumers as Pakistan does not import petrol every day • Sharjeel urges MQM-P to press federal govt for withdrawal of Rs100-plus petroleum levy KARACHI: The Sindh Assembly, otherwise divided along bitter party lines, on Tuesday unanimously demanded through a resolution that the federal government immediately stop the practice of increasing petroleum prices on a daily basis, saying that no new shipment or import of petrol arrives in the country every day to justify it. The resolution, tabled by Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) lawmaker Muhammad Owais, said that daily fluctuations in international oil prices should not be passed on to consumers on a daily basis, as Pakistan did not import petrol daily. The resolution said that the continuous increase in petrol prices was fuelling inflation and the common man was facing severe hardship. It said, “This House demands that the federal government immediately stop the daily increase in petroleum product prices,” adding that no new shipment or import of petrol arrived in Pakistan on a daily basis to justify passing on daily fluctuations in international prices. The resolution demanded that stability be brought to petroleum prices to provide relief to the public and that the practice of daily price hikes be ended forthwith. This was the second adopted resolution related to petroleum products in the current session of the assembly. Speaking on his resolution, the PTI member also demanded the withdrawal of the Rs100-plus petroleum levy through a unanimously adopted resolution. Supporting the resolution, Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon said that people were distressed due to rising petroleum prices and the federal government was charging over Rs100 per litre as a levy, which should be withdrawn. He asked the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), an ally of the federal government, to take up the issue with the Centre to provide relief to the people. Recalling that the MQM had once quit the PPP-led federal government in 2008 over a one-rupee increase in petrol price, he said the party was now silently enjoying power. “Those who are sitting in the federal cabinet should speak on this issue,” he said. The senior minister said that the PPP fully supported the resolution and demanded that the federal government abolish the levy and “come to its senses” on petroleum pricing. He said that MQM-P’s federal representatives should explain why they were not raising their voice against petroleum inflation. ‘PM’s Rs100 subsidy on petrol not sufficient’ Later, speaking to reporters at the Media Corner on the premises of the assembly, provincial government spokesperson Sadia Javed said the federal government’s plan to give a Rs100 subsidy on petrol for certain categories was not sufficient and would not benefit the poor. She said that the prime minister should improve the FBR’s performance and reduce the Rs125 per litre tax on petrol, as only a direct cut in prices would provide genuine relief. She argued that petrol was not used only by the elite but also by goods transport, and unless transport costs came down, food prices would not fall. Ms Javed also lashed out at Federal Minister Mustafa Kamal, terming him “extremely ill-mannered” for cursing politics, and said that if he hated politics so much he should quit politics and resign from his ministry. She questioned why he had not resigned over the deaths of children at PIMS Hospital. Adjournment motion During proceedings, an adjournment motion by MQM-P MPA Amir Siddiqui regarding the sale of narcotics under flyovers and bridges was rejected by a member of the Panel of Chairmen, Dr Sikandar Shoro, after opposition from the government. Mr Siddiqui said that drugs were being sold openly under flyovers and bridges. He said that the menace was also affecting educational institutions, including schools and colleges. PPP MPA Heer Soho opposed the motion, saying an adjournment motion had to relate to a recent occurrence and the motion did not meet the criteria. Education Minister said the assembly’s standing committee on home had already taken up the issue and action was being taken in this regard. “Let the result come,” he said. Excise Minister Mukesh Chawala also opposed the adjournment motion, saying that the house had already debated the issue at length and the government was working to contain the menace. The chair said that the motion was not maintainable and ruled it out of order. Question Hour Earlier, during the Question Hour, Women Development Minister Shaheena Sher Ali said that complaint centres were functioning at the divisional level across the province and offices were also set up in every district. “Five to 15 complaints were received daily, and prompt action was taken on them,” she added. The minister said that women were being imparted training through a revolving fund and two day-care centres were functioning in Karachi with a prescribed age limit for admission. “Awareness is being created about helpline 1094,” she added. Replying to a question, she said there was no day-care centre inside the Sindh Assembly, but one was functioning near the Karachi Press Club. Dr Sikandar Shoro, who was presiding over the sitting as a member of the Panel of Chairmen, observed that the assembly should also have a day-care centre. The minister said that the department would establish one if space was provided. Several other items on the assembly business agenda, including three other resolutions and as many private motions of the opposition members, did not come up as the house was adjourned immediately after the unanimous passage of the resolution against the petroleum levy. The house was later adjourned till Friday. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

Employee claims facing police ire for saying Mir Raza didn’t use drugs. KARACHI: An employee of businessman Mir Raza Ali told a judicial commission on Tuesday that he faced investigators’ anger after saying the deceased did not use drugs. The Judicial Commission in the Mir Raza murder case continued its proceedings on Tuesday and recorded statements of a police officer, an employee of the deceased and his two investors. The one-member commission headed by Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court also expressed displeasure over a focal person of the provincial government and police for still not providing the complete record of the case to the commission despite repeated directives. In his testimony, the manager of the victim’s eatery Wafflix, Shahryar, said that he was working at the Bahadurabad branch for the last two years and reporting to the victim who treated him like a younger brother. Wafflix manager tells judicial commission parts of his police statements were ‘incorrectly’ attributed to him Responding to a question of the commission about losses to the business of the deceased, he deposed that the sales had been declining for the past few months and the salaries of the staff were also delayed during the last couple of months, but he did not find the victim worried during his last interactions with him. He said that the daily sales were around Rs100,000, but they had fallen to Rs75,000 to Rs70,000 during the last two months. He also said that police had recorded his statements twice and his phone was also seized by the second investigation team on Aug 17, adding that his first statement was written on a paper on Aug 2 and the second testimony was recorded through video. The witness further submitted that the police had asked questions about the business and the family issues of the victim. He said the first team had misbehaved with him while SP Qais, who is said to be a part of the second team, had also come down hard on him when he had informed the team that the victim was not using any drugs. The commission pointed out that he had provided complete details and figures about the business of the deceased to the police, but did not provide the same to the commission, which contradicted his testimonies recorded by the police. He submitted that the police did not read out such statements to him and some additions were incorrectly attributed to him. The manager also deposed that the victim along with his business partner Ahmed Bhardey had gone to Hyderabad to attend a party arranged by a catering firm on July 25 and came back on the following day while the victim had taken Rs29,000 from him around midnight of July 27 and left the branch. He further testified that he had closed the branch on the same night around 3:30am and at around 4:10am Bhardey had asked him regarding Raza’s whereabouts. He maintained that on July 28, another employee had informed him that a pistol of a security guard of the eatery, kept at the shop, was missing and they came to know through the footage that Raza came to the branch last night after it was closed and took the weapon. However, he said that as per his knowledge, the victim had never used any weapon and he had no dispute with any vendor, creditor or investor. At the outset of the hearing, Inspector Muhammad Ali turned up and deposed that he was posted at the investigation section of District South and co-opted by the current police team investigating the case as it was his responsibility to assist the team. He also said that he was told to file a letter when he had gone to collect the post-mortem report from the hospital and despite submitting the letter, he did not get the report since the officer concerned was said to be out of the city. Replying to a query of the commission, the police officer further testified that the investigating officer had gone to Hyderabad when he had sought the autopsy report in order to submit it to the investigation team. Muhammad Hassan Khan Tanoli, who recorded his statement via video link from Australia, said that he and Raza had been friends since school and initially, he had provided Rs500,000 to the victim and he had returned the same within the given period along with some profit. Thereafter, he also deposed that he had given him Rs7.5 million as he was willing to import containers of chocolates as well as expanding business. The victim had handed over some cheques to him and advised him not to deposit them since he would arrange the money. The witness further testified that he had contacted Ahmed Bhardey through social media after Raza had gone missing and later also spoke to the father of the victim. The commission asked him that Mr Bhardey in his statement said that he (Hassan) had demanded the return of the money in question from him. He replied that he had only informed the business partner of the victim that he had provided money or a loan to Raza. He had admitted that the victim had borrowed such money for Wafflix while Bhardey had claimed that he was not aware of such an investment. Asad Ali Butt deposed that he had first met the victim in 2016-17 and he had established an outlet in Bahadurabad in 2022 and he had also encouraged people to invest in it. He also said that he had also made an investment of Rs2.5m with Wafflix and all the transactions were made through the account of his mother. During the hearing, the counsel for Raza’s family Jibran Nasir informed the commission that the victim’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, had received a phone call last night and the caller had identified himself as a security official of an institution. The counsel said that the caller had asked Mir Hussain whether he suspected Ahmed Bhardey and Abdullah Bhardey or Asif and his brother Abid as the accused persons. However, he told the caller that the matter was being investigated by the police and therefore, the caller expressed displeasure and disconnected the call, he added. The lawyer said that he has submitted the screenshots and call recording to the registrar of the commission. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

Politics and protests. IT is the same tired play. As soon as the opposition announces a protest, the government reflexively cracks down. Citizens are roughed up and arrested, and the security officials who round them up later collect medals for their services. There are no consequences for this abuse of state power. Indeed, it increasingly appears that the lead-up to a protest, and not the protest itself, is where the real political battle is fought. And all this is playing out at the moment on television screens and social media, as the PTI prepares for its Sept 27 march on Islamabad to demand its jailed founder’s release. The machinery of the state has kicked into action all over the country, armed with the usual pretexts of ‘prevention of violence’ and ‘protection of public infrastructure and property’. The actions taken to thwart the march appear to be many. At least 155, perhaps more, preventive detention orders have been issued under the MPO; lists have been drawn up of PTI leaders and workers for further ‘preventive arrests’; police personnel’s leaves have been cancelled; containers and roadblocks are being prepared ; restrictions have been placed on rallies and public gatherings; and Section 144 has been implemented in Punjab , with plans of a broader rollout soon. Authorities undoubtedly have a responsibility to maintain order, and reasonable measures to discharge that responsibility are legitimate. But half a dozen overlapping instruments, deployed against a political party’s leadership and rank and file, cannot be considered reasonable by any stretch. Sadly, such actions only give the impression that even calls for protest are considered a thought crime in our society. The heavy-handedness with which the government has been curtailing the opposition’s ability to exercise its lawful political rights should not be overlooked. Every democracy allows its citizens to express their will in different ways, including through peaceful public protests. That the government can and will prosecute political leaders and workers who actually break the law is not in dispute; the state has every right to respond firmly when violent protest tactics are employed deliberately. However, the point is that deterrents already exist and do not require the pre-emptive detention of people who have broken no law. Past protests may have turned violent, but that history cannot be used as a justification to arbitrarily suspend constitutional rights for those who have caused no offence. It is time to stop treating dissent as a security threat and allow the public a peaceful outlet to air its grievances. The consequences of not ceding that space gracefully will only grow more severe with time. A government confident in its own legitimacy does not need to criminalise the mere anticipation of a protest. Ours, evidently, is not that confident. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

Dangerous escalation. JUST weeks after its formation, the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement faces its first challenge: the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi militia . The rebel group has struck Saudi air bases and key oil facilities with missiles and drones, while the kingdom has intensified air strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthis formally declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting Saudi-flagged shipping, after Yemeni government forces attacked a flight from Iran at Sana’a airport. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2014. The violence subsided after the warring sides reached an internationally brokered ceasefire in 2022, but flared up again after the July incident when the militia broke the truce, declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and began attacking Saudi vessels. Its ultimate aim is to drive Saudi Arabia out of Yemen and take full control of the territory. This latest escalation has widened the conflict in West Asia, even as America’s war with Iran grinds on with no end in sight. With the fighting now threatening Saudi Arabia directly, will the kingdom invoke the alliance’s mutual defence clause — the one that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all members? The danger of a wider conflagration engulfing the entire region carries serious implications for the rest of the world. The Houthis, who already hold much of Yemen, have seized a strategic island in a lightning offensive against government forces, giving them complete control of Bab al-Mandeb — the key marine chokepoint through which 12 per cent of the world’s trade passes. They now control 90 per cent of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. The Houthi leadership says it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked vessels. But the heightening tension is likely to keep other ships away. With the Strait of Hormuz virtually blocked, the situation is explosive. Global energy markets, already reeling from the six-month conflict between US-Israel and Iran, are bracing for further shock. Saudi Arabia, which had stayed out of the Iran war, now risks being drawn into a wider conflict. These actions by a militia widely seen as aligned with Iran have opened a new front in the conflict. They have coincided with a drone attack, apparently launched from Iraq by allegedly another Iran-linked militia, that forced temporary closure of the East-West oil pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia. Together, the attacks have disrupted Saudi oil exports. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, though the group also operates independently of Tehran. The attacks on Saudi Arabia are certainly not in Iran’s interest while it is engaged in an existential war with the US — the fallout is already visible. Saudi Arabia, which had so far kept itself out of the Iran war, is now in danger of being drawn into a wider regional conflict. Although Iran has distanced itself from the attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure by the two militias, the incidents have heightened tensions between Riyadh and Tehran. Following the attacks, talks between Iran and the Gulf states aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz were postponed . It would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member states in two years; the meeting, to be held in Oman, was part of an effort to find a regional solution allowing free passage through the critical waterway. The latest flare-up has thwarted that effort. As the fighting spreads, Saudi Arabia finds itself on the front line. In the latest turn, the kingdom reportedly sought American military help , only to be turned down by President Donald Trump, who said the Houthis had assured him they did not want to expand the conflict. The development has given an intriguing twist to the conflict. Trump’s response is said to be driven by his frustration with the kingdom for failing to actively support his war against Iran. America and Israel have carried out missile strikes against the Houthis in the past over their support for the Palestinian resistance. But there is also the question of whether US intervention in the Saudi-Houthi conflict will help stabilise a situation for which Washington is itself responsible. The growing tension between Iran and Saudi Ara­bia will only serve the US agenda in the region. So far, Saudi Arabia has not formally invoked the Makkah defence alliance clause, which would require Pakistan and Turkiye to come to its def­ence if it is attacked. But consultations are under way as the conflict spreads. Diplomatic efforts to halt the Houthis’ escalatory moves are still continuing. Reportedly, Pakistan’s military chief and the Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan both spoke to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan is also believed to have conveyed a Saudi message urging Iran to rein in the Houthis, and reminded Tehran of Islamabad’s own pact commitment to Riyadh. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif recently said that unprovoked aggression against the kingdom, or a spillover into it, would make the pact operational — “there should be no doubt about that”. Earlier, in April 2026, Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry announced that a Pakistani military contingent had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base, with fighter and support aircraft, under a bilateral defence pact signed in September 2025 . Following Khawaja Asif’s remarks, however, the Foreign Office spokesperson said , “I don’t think we should be discussing this topic in the context of its operationalisation”. The situation remains dangerous for both Pakistan and the larger region, and the widening conflict could suck in even those countries that have kept out of the Iran war and have been trying to help broker a negotiated end to it. Pakistan needs to tread a more cautious path in a conflict that could prove disastrous for the country. It’s a perilous escalation that needs to be resolved through negotiations rather than war. Karachi: how much dirtier?. AS they say everything comes at a cost — and so does Karachi’s ranking as one of the least liveable cities. Karachi has slipped from the seventh least liveable city in 2021 to the fourth least liveable one in 2026. It ranks 170th among the 173 cities surveyed by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). This decline has come despite enormous spending by the Sindh government — estimated at around Rs126 billion in these five years alone — to garbage-collection contractors. Since 2017, including the current year’s allocation, spending on garbage collection and street sweeping is estimated to exceed Rs190bn, with an estimated Rs160-170bn spent in the name of Karachi alone. No other initiative has received such generous provincial financing over the past decade — not the BRT Red Line, the BRT Yellow Line, the K-IV water supply project, the Safe City project, Karachi’s road network, not even the Right Bank Outfall Drain, which is critical to rural Sindh’s economy. When the EIU measures liveability, environmental quality is only one of five major criteria, with cleanliness forming a sub-component. However, on Numbeo’s global pollution index, Karachi continues to rank as one of the world’s most polluted cities with a pollution index score of 89.5/100. This index evaluates air quality, drinking water availability, garbage disposal, cleanliness, water pollution, noise and light pollution, green spaces, and overall comfort. Across all these metrics, garbage disposal has remained the poorest performer despite billions being spent by the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board (SSWMB) under the chief minister’s chairmanship. In 2016, the Sindh government took over the mu­­nicipal functions of garbage collection and stre­­et sweeping — previously managed by the KMC and union councils — and outsourced them to foreign firms. The contracts covered door-to-door collection, sweeping of streets, lanes, medians, footpaths and open spaces, transportation to transfer stations and landfills, provision of bins and compactors, deployment of sanitary workers, and GPS-based monitoring. Initially introduced across Karachi’s districts, the outsourcing model was later extended to Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana. The city’s dismal ranking on the liveability and pollution indexes reflects a crisis of governance more than a shortage of funds. The system was designed around a simple principle: garbage should not remain on the ground. Mini-trucks were to collect waste door to door and from designated bins, feed it into compactors at district collection centres, and ensure its transportation to landfill sites the same day. Uncollected areas, roadside garbage, failure to deploy prescri­bed staff or machinery, and other performance lap­­­­ses attracted financial penalties. Vehicles were to be GPS-tracked, while manual sweeping supplemented mechanical cleaning. A command-and-control system linked to the SSWMB headquarters was to monitor fleet movements; an independent firm was to verify the contractors’ performan­ce; and complaints were to be resolved within eight hours. Going by these performance indicators — and an estimated public-sector price tag approaching Rs170bn for the city over the period — Karachi should have become one of the cleanest cities in the region during the past decade. Yet the reality across much of the city is different. Open plots continue to serve as informal garbage dumps. Door-to-door collection remains patchy or is altogether absent in many localities. Waste continues to accumulate along the roads, open spaces and drains. Elected representatives themselves frequently complain about inadequate responsiveness by solid-waste contractors. Karachi continues to be ranked as one of the dirtiest cities all these 10 years. A review of these contracts against the ground realities over the past decade suggests that strict enforcement of the built-in penalty clauses should have driven non-compliant contractors into bankruptcy. The obvious question is: how have contractors been able to operate with such visible gaps between contractual obligations and conditions on the ground? The answer lies in two major contract and statutory violations by the provincial administration itself. First, the Sindh government has failed to hire an independent consulting firm for third-party verification since 2017, effectively granting contractors a decade-long exemption from performance audits. Second, the government has bypassed Section 14(3) of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Act, 2021, which states: “The executive directors of the board shall be appointed by the chief minister either from cadre service officers working under the control of government having relevant professional qualification and experience or from private sector through a competitive process possessing the requisite qualifications and experience of the post.” Despite managing contracts valued at Rs30-40bn, a key oversight position, such as director mo­­nito­ring and evaluation, has been filled by an of­­f­icer from the Benazir Income Support Prog­ram­­me. Compounding the issue is the lack of parliame­nt­a­­ry oversight. Reports from the Auditor General of Pakistan from 2018 through 2025 have repeatedly highlighted losses of billions of rupees by the SSWMB due to payments made without third-par­­ty verification, uncollected penalties, in­­ade­quate staffing, and overpayments. Yet, no effective corrective action has been taken all these years. The State of Governance in Pakistan, 2023, based on a nationwide household survey by TDEA/ Fafen, found 65 per cent of Karachi respondents to be dissatisfied with garbage disposal services, while another 22pc had no service available in their locality. So, 87pc of Karachi households surveyed were either dissatisfied with garbage disposal or had no service — a remarkable outcome after years of outsourcing and billions of rupees spent on solid-waste management. After chairing the board for seven years, starting in 2014, the chief minister transferred the steering committee to the local government minister in 2021, and operational supervision was handed to the mayor of Karachi in 2024. However, meaningful coordination with elected town chairmen and union councils to hold contractors accountable remains absent. In fact, despite their poor performance, SSWMB contractors were rewarded with a 42pc increase in payment, raising their annual bill from Rs28.3bn in 2024-25 to Rs40.3bn in 2025-26. Like many of Karachi’s challenges, the real bottleneck has not been the shortage of funds for the Sindh government, but poor governance and lack of accountability. With the country’s economic engine ranking among the lowest on the liveability index and among the highest on the pollution index, all our aspirations for the country’s progress will remain a pipe dream. The writer is former federal secretary, caretaker provincial minister and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

Imran’s sisters, lawyers denied meeting at Adiala. • Aleema says KP should not accord protocol to Nawaz during his visits to province • PTI information secretary rejects FCC’s decision to seek SC record on ex-PM’s proposed hospital transfer ISLAMABAD:While Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has been facing a “tough time” in Lahore , Imran Khan’s sister Aleema Khan on Tuesday suggested that protocol should not be accorded to former prime minister Nawaz Sharif during his visits to KP. She was speaking to media persons outside Adiala jail after, once again, she was not allowed to meet her brother in violation of the Isla­mabad High Court’s (IHC) orders. Advocate Awais Younas Chau­dhry, who submits lists of leaders and lawyers to the jail administration seeking permission to meet Imran Khan, told Dawn that his sisters and six lawyers reached outside Adiala jail but were not allowed to meet the PTI founder. “The sisters waited there even after 6:30pm, but they were not informed about the approval of the meeting. The IHC has ordered that meetings of the family and lawyers with Imran Khan be arranged on Tuesdays and meetings of party leaders on Thursdays, but the court orders are being violated,” he said. Ms Khan, while talking to media persons, claimed that the ruling elite was scared and was preparing to flee the country. When asked about the IHC’s orders that roads should not be blocked during protests, she said: “You will see that the government will itself close the roads. After that, IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar should call the government and ask it to open the roads,” she suggested. Replying to a question, Ms Khan said she would suggest that Justice Sarfraz Dogar summon her if she was committing contempt of court. Another sister of Imran Khan, Dr Uzma Khan, said the judges had insulted the whole country, but the media was asking whether the sisters had disgraced the judiciary. Replying to a question, Aleema Khan said the constitutional court had been established unconstitutionally. “We were not aware of their names, but due to social media, now we know them very well. Justice Baqar Najafi sent Nawaz Sharif abroad on a Rs50 stamp paper and forgot to ask why he was not returning. Now he has been worrying that Imran Khan should not come out of jail,” she added. She said the constitutional court had been established to undermine the Supreme Court (SC) and that its aim was to keep Imran Khan in jail. “It is necessary for the SC to ensure its survival and integrity,” she suggested. She said she had suggested to Sohail Afridi that he make two demands: first, that Imran Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital, as those who had put him in jail were allegedly involved in attempts to kill him; and second, that Justice Dogar should start hearing Imran Khan’s bail applications. When asked about the KP chief minister having a “tough time” in Lahore, she said that, in response, the KP government should not accord protocol to Nawaz Sharif during his visits to the province. FCC decision Meanwhile, PTI Central Infor­m­ation Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram rejected the Federal Cons­titutional Court’s (FCC) decision to summon from the SC the record of the case concerning PTI founder Imran Khan’s transfer to a hospital, calling the move a blatant manifestation of how the top court had been deliberately weakened and rendered virtually ineffective throu­gh the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments. Mr Akram urged the FCC to exercise the utmost restraint and refrain from interfering in matters already pending before the SC, the country’s apex judicial forum. President Asif Ali Zardari on Wednesday gave his approval for conferring the Tamgha-i-Shujaat on Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) nurse Razia Noreen, who saved the life of a newborn during a fire at the facility that killed 14 infants. The announcement was made by the Presidency. It added that the president had also approved several bills, including the National Institute of Folk and Traditional Heritage (Lok Virsa) Amendment Bill, 2026, the Standard Time (Interpretation of References) Amendment Bill, 2026, and another related to the management of hazardous materials in ships. The incident raised concerns over fire safety measures and sparked calls for accountability , with criminal action being ordered against eight officials . She then attempted to re-enter the nursery shortly afterwards, but the fire had spread by then. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had awarded Noreen a Rs10 million cheque in recognition of her extraordinary bravery and sense of duty. Saudi-led coalition says Houthis targeted Makkah with drone, warns of 'red line'. The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels on Wednesday of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route. The Houthis swiftly rejected as a “lie” Riyadh’s report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year. “The claims about targeting Makkah are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis’ politburo wrote on X. The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a “red line”. “The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia,” the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) — a bloc of 57 Muslim countries — condemned the “heinous” attack. Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Makkah and across swathes of the kingdom’s south, which borders Yemen. The alerts, including the first one issued in Makkah since the Middle East war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom’s south. Fighting flared in July when the Houthis, who have for years controlled swathes of northern Yemen, launched a large-scale offensive against Yemeni government forces. The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula’s poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the United Nations. Yemen’s permanent representative at the UN, Abdullah al-Saadi, said Yemenis were fighting to restore “national institutions across every inch of their land”, and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis. PM Shehbaz condemns ‘dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack’ Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned in the “strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack against the Holy Site of Makkah Al-Mukarramah”. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act. There can be no words strong enough to capture the depth of anguish and sorrow felt by us at this reprehensible and unforgivable act,” he wrote in a post on X. He lauded the “extraordinary vigilance, courage, and professionalism of the Royal Saudi Armed Forces for their swift and heroic action”. The premier urged “all parties to exercise maximum restraint and to step back from the brink of further escalation”. “Our region has already suffered far too much from conflict. Dialogue and diplomacy remain the only sustainable path towards peace,” he stressed. “Pakistan stands unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder with the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in the defence of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as for the security and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain — a duty that every Pakistani carries close to their heart.” ‘Hostile and extremist’ On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia and Egypt called for free navigation in the Red Sea following the Houthis’ offensive in the vital waterway. After meeting in Cairo, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called for “ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation” through the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, the Egyptian presidency said. The revival of Yemen’s civil war , dormant since 2022, has left Riyadh rushing to respond. US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but was turned down. The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab al-Mandab except for Saudi vessels. Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers. Disruption in the strait could cause Egypt to feel the pinch too, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, upon which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue. Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel’s war on Gaza. On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab al-Mandab was closed, saying it would be “catastrophic for the entire world”. The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s leading crude exporter, helping push global prices above the $100-a-barrel threshold. The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks “firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom”, and would take “all necessary operational measures to deter this … hostile and extremist approach”. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Tuesday that Saudi Arabia launched 52 airstrikes on Yemen over the past 24 hours, accusing it of targeting civilian sites, including schools and bridges. But Riyadh’s strikes have failed to reverse the group’s gains. A US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.

DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no regional aspirations', intended for collective deterrence. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that the Makkah Defence Alliance — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English ’s ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the programme’s host, Tom Burges Watson. During the show, aired during the early hours of Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked what the agreement committed Pakistan to. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains for collective deterrence and defence of the three countries,” he said. Watson then asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. Elaborating further, he said the countries part of the alliance had independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances. “So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he added. At that, Watson asked, “But does it contain any mutual defence obligation?” In his short reply to the question, Lt Gen Chaudhry remarked, “The text that has been made public by the leadership of the three countries enunciates that very clearly and it’s interpretation is quite clear.” Asked how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalisation of defensive commitments were never made public in any discourse. “You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details […] What you’re asking is the how part — that how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression. “That is always part of the operational classification and security […] What you’re asking is that how it will be done. It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualise it,” he said. When specifically asked whether the military spokesperson saw the alliance “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s relationship with China, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that it complemented Islamabad-Beijing ties. “We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Turkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it, that how historic these relationships are. We have formalised that. “Nobody has any problem with that. Everyone understands that this is defensive; everyone understand it is for maintaining stability and peace in the region; and all the three countries that are part of it they have a wonderful relationship with China,” he said. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have the shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained. US-Iran mediation and Pakistan’s ‘unique position’ During his interview to Watson, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about Pakistan’s efforts for mediation between the US and Iran and whether the Makkah Defence Alliance complicated Pakistan’s position towards Tehran. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied such was not the case, adding that the alliance was based on decades-old strategic ties. “This alliance is a formalisation of that strategic relationship in a peculiar environment,” he said, adding that the pact was based on collective deterrence. The defence pact, he said, had no offensive or aggressive element and was purely defensive in nature. Asked why Pakistan had opted to play the role of a mediator in the ongoing Middle East conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran late in February, he succinctly stated, “For regional peace”. Lt Gen Chaudhry then added that stability stemmed from peace and Pakistan was a proponent of peace on the region. Moreover, he continued, Pakistan had a “unique position” in this case because of its policy of alignment and engagement with countries across the world. Hence, it could play the role of an “objective arbiter of peace and an honest broker of peace”. To a question about progress on the mediation front and towards a settlement, Lt Gen Chaudhry explained that one of the prerequisites of good mediation was remaining objective and neutral. “So it’s not for us as a mediator to start commenting on things that are happening or that are bound to happen,” he said, adding that Pakistan’s political and military leadership had been reaching out to all the parties so that “better sense prevails and, instead of a military solution, we come to a negotiated outcome of this very complex situation”. Watson then pointed to the possibility of the US and Iran rejecting Pakistan’s proposal and asked whether Islamabad was prepared to continue its mediation in that case. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied, “Is there any other way of resolving this conflict other than [through] mediation?” Is there any other desirable way of doing that?” He stressed the need for a “negotiated, peaceful outcome”, adding that those who could mediate objectively and sincerely between the two sides, they must continue their efforts. Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the conflict spilling over towards its western frontiers, Lt Gen Chaudhry answered that as far as Pakistan’s borders, territorial integrity and sovereignty was concerned, “we are very confident and very self-reliant on our security”. There were always concerns of any conflict spiralling horizontally or vertically, he said, adding that not just Pakistan, but the entire and the world at large was feeling the impact of the conflict. “So, there are [always] concerns in multiple domains,” but Pakistan was “fully confident of taking care of whatever nefarious designs come out of that towards” it, he said. When asked whether Pakistan aimed to become a regional mediator or was simply trying to prevent a regional war from reaching its own doorstep, Lt Gen Chaudhry responded, “Pakistan is interested in regional peace and stability, because peace and stability is essential for development, for human development, for prosperity and for the citizens of Pakistan and the region.” And if the “mediation is for peace, […] and we’ll always be there”. Tuvalu and Taiwan 'like brothers', President Lai Ching-te says. Tuvalu's Foreign Affairs Minister Paulson Panapa has met with Taiwan president Lai Ching-te this week.
Fiji declares HIV emergency as 1 in 60 Fijian adults live with HIV. One in 60 Fijian adults are now living with HIV.
Super Rugby Pacific: Fijian Drua to host eight home games in 2027. The Fiji-based franchise will also host Super Rugby Pacific defending champions, the Hurricanes, in Suva in April next year.

Panguna attack: PNG minister claims Indian miner was warned against investing in Bougainville. Papua New Guinea's trade minister claims he warned the Indian mining company that was attacked at Panguna on Sunday not to invest in Bougainville.
Data from more than 600 people shows resting heart rates have their own secret rhythm. The rhythms aren’t necessarily tied to hormones, nor any other single cause.

Imported phosphate for fertiliser is expensive – could this homegrown alternative be a solution?. Research shows a phosphorus-rich compound found in wastewater raises uptake by plants and reduces discharge to waterways.

Democrats’ chances of gaining control of Congress at US midterms depend on Iran war. Recent polling shows if the disruption caused by the Trump administration’s war with Iran continues, Democrats will likely gain control of Congress.

Shocks, alchemy and John Howard’s ‘long shadow’ have shaped 21st century Australian politics. New books by George Megalogenis and Paul Strangio consider 21st century Australia: a time of rapid social change with many politicians stuck ‘in a white-bloke past’.

View from The Hill: One Nation would have more people leaving than entering Australia over three years. One Nation has released a radical policy that would see Australia reduce its temporary migrant population by 750,000.

Why strengthening ties with the Global South was a top priority for Putin’s recent diplomacy blitz. The Ukraine war certainly featured in conversations. Tellingly, however, Putin steered many talks with leaders towards fuel, trade and transit.
Why big tech will hate the Australian tax office’s latest ruling. Australia’s laws don’t deal with all the ways local profits are shifted offshore. The ATO aims to close that gap.

Big AI wants to slow down AI research. Is it a safety pause or a strategic retreat?. AI companies are calling for a coordinated pause to progress – but making it work, and keeping AI safe, won’t be easy.

Rinse: Amrita Hepi’s show about beginnings is a mid-career masterpiece. The internationally acclaimed fusion of choreography and monologue, co-created by Hepi with Mish Grigor, is a witty exploration of beginnings.
Trailblazing lawyer Mary Gaudron, a woman of many firsts, leaves a huge and lasting legacy. The first woman judge on the High Court shaped Australian legal history and was an inspiration to many.

All-round condemnation for Pauline Hanson over Indigenous slur. Pauline Hanson’s derogatory remarks about Indigenous people on a podcast last year have been slammed by members of the government, the Liberals and the Nationals.

Five years into AUKUS, what do we have to show for it? We’ve measured progress on three key metrics. Though reliably measuring progress is difficult, it would be disingenuous to say Australia has nothing to show for its investments to date.

Unsustainable – or manageable? We don’t yet know how data centres will impact Australia’s environment. The data centre boom will mean more energy and water use. The real question is how the energy is produced – and where the water comes from.

Australia’s digital duty of care bill needs these three changes to tackle online child sexual exploitation. Tech platforms need to be responsible for reporting online child sexual exploitation rather than relying on victims to do so.

Make ‘em laugh: how One Nation uses comedy to normalise harmful ideas. The party’s Please Explain cartoon series has ignited a political firestorm, but behind the punchlines and backlash is an insidious way to spread propaganda.
Australia’s female economists have been making history for nearly 150 years. It’s time we knew their stories. In a stubbornly male dominated field, how brilliant did a woman have to be to succeed?

It’s been one year since Australia assessed its national climate risk. But have we listened?. Over the past 12 months, the federal government has approved multiple fossil fuel projects and cut climate science funding.

1 in 3 uni students experience serious financial hardship. Could concession cards for all help?. The peak body for Australian universities says the measure would ease cost-of-living pressures for students.

Skipping showers is the latest trend. But is there any science to ‘pheromone’ maxxing?. Animals use pheromones as chemical messengers to attract a mate or mark territory. But human sweat is very different.

Poetry is popular with young Australians, from pop-up readings to poetry slams. Young poets are performing at poetry slams, pop-up events and salons around Australia – and publishing, too. Who are they – and why is poetry so popular?

‘Buy now, pay later’ doesn’t feel like debt. For young people, that can be a big problem. A survey of young New Zealanders finds four in ten didn’t view buy now, pay later as debt. That perception can influence how they use it.

The case for NZ joining the UK in sanctioning Israel over illegal West Bank settlements. The government insists sanctioning Israel is too complex so close to an election. But New Zealand also has obligations under international law it shouldn’t ignore.

Coalition retains clear lead in Victorian Resolve poll, while federal polls are mixed. Labor is likely to lose the Victorian election, but it’s unclear whether the Coalition will be able to govern in majority or need support from One Nation.

Our new research shows humans have maligned bandicoots for decades, making them more vulnerable to extinction. Humans have had a complex relationship with this marsupial, known for its pointy snout, thin tail and large hind feet.

How does unthinkable policy become inevitable? The ‘Overton window’ is one possible answer. It was once deemed crazy to get rid of protective tariffs. Privatising state banks was inconceivable. Both are now commonplace, but how does this happen?

Why Sydney Sweeney’s controversial advert goes beyond sexualising women’s sport. The discussion surrounding the American actor’s ad raises bigger questions about the attention placed on women’s bodies, not just in sport.

Bluster and betrayal: Paul Barry probes how steel tycoon Sanjeev Gupta hoodwinked the powerful. Amid news that 500 jobs will go at the Whyalla steelworks, once owned by Gupta’s GFG Alliance, The Big Steal is a powerful – and timely – work of journalism.

Was there really a female king in ancient Egypt 5,000 years ago? New study says yes. Meretneith was buried in a tomb fit for a male ruler. But for decades, debate has raged over her true royal status.

Poorly fitting sports bras are forcing some women and girls away from sport – new research. Most decision-makers in sport think girls and women would benefit from learning about sports bra design, fit and support. Less than 1% offer this education.

David Hockney: Portraits in Print reveals lesser-known aspects of the celebrated artist. The National Gallery of Australia exhibition showcases the late British artist’s mastery of intimate detail and talent for connection.
Hanson ‘regrets’ hurt caused by remark about ‘primitive’ First Nations people. After facing a barrage of criticism for her comments, the One Nation leader says it was not her intention to cause hurt.

175 years of university architecture reflects Australian history. We shouldn’t let that history be lost. University campuses reflect the layers of architectural and landscape styles that have shaped our cities and suburbs.

AFP commissioner urges ‘conversation’ about link between Australians’ level of illicit drug use and organised crime. Krissy Barrett’s call comes after recent murders in Sydney linked to organised crime included two cases of mistaken identity in one week.

More than 2 million Indigenous people lived in Australia in 1788: new research. Genetic, archaeological and environmental evidence suggest the Indigenous population fell by more than 90% in the 70 years after the British invaded.

Incorporation law gave Big Tech state-like power. Can it now help rein it in?. Governments can curb corporate power. But first we need to understand how corporate law allows private ventures to accumulate power that can endure for generations.

How would One Nation’s immigration plan affect the labour market and economy?. Reducing the number of people on student and graduate visas may reduce migration numbers, but it could also weaken demand for Australian goods and services.

Bird flu has claimed its first Australian sea lion and dolphin. How does the virus get into these animals?. How does a dolphin or seal even get bird flu? Most likely through contact with sick birds – or eating their carcasses.

Australia’s data centre build-out carries risks for the economy – and inflation. The rush to build data centres brings investment and the promise of a sophisticated digital economy. But it also creates new pressure on housing and skilled workers.
Is pasta a type of noodle? The surprisingly serious debate over two beloved carbs. Like many food debates, this one is tangled up in culture, history and power.

How does the menopause drug Veoza work? And how is it different to hormone therapy?. Some women can’t take hormone replacement therapy to alleviate hot flashes and night sweats. This medication is one alternative.

The government might strip some asylum seekers of their work rights. Here’s why it shouldn’t. The government is reportedly considering restricting the work rights of asylum seekers as part of its plan to decrease migration. But it’s not a good idea.

Do pimple patches actually work? Here’s what the science says. If you’re squeamish, you might want to avoid the TikTok videos of people peeling off their pimple patches. But if you want to know if they really work, read on.
Should schools ban students from doing cartwheels?. Some schools are reportedly restricting cartwheels and handstands to prevent injuries.

Naomi Klein’s new book calls out end times fascism. What is this – and what’s the role of big tech?. Two new books, End Times Fascism and Nerd Reich, take a hard look at fascism today – and its intersections with big tech.

Is the nuclear non-proliferation pact a model for regulating runaway AI?. Competition for AI dominance resembles the nuclear arms race of the Cold War era. A similarly serious response may also now be needed.
Climate change is putting the squeeze on the world’s grapegrowers: new research. Renowned wine regions from Australia to South Africa are battling increasingly fierce fire seasons.

The Houthis have further tightened their grip on the Red Sea. Here’s what it could mean for the world. The move suggests Iran and its allies are settling in for a long war. That could mean pain for the global economy.

The Jim Henson Company reminds us even the synthetic can be joyous and beautiful and beloved. Make, Believe, Magic: The Worlds of The Jim Henson Company is now open at QAGOMA, Brisbane. It reminds us that puppets are extensions of us.
The US says it has launched ‘space control weapons’. It plays into the hands of its enemies. This could mark the start of a major arms race in space, which would threaten all of us on Earth.

Hanson’s personal attacks and offensive comments are straight out of the populist playbook. But they come with risks. What is acceptable from a minor party of protest may not be what voters want to see from a potential government.

On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/11/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 11 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky E-post Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Spara Utskrift 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country.
